::: {.callout-note appearance='simple' collapse=true}
## Source

The topics of this chapter follow the course calendar,
and their order follows Kameron Decker Harris's Fall 2026 lecture notes on trees.
These come from those notes:

- a tree as a connected graph with no cycles (the notes say no simple circuits), and a forest, whose connected components are trees;
- the theorem that a graph is a tree if and only if there is exactly one path between every two of its vertices;
- rooted trees, with the root, parents, children, ancestors, descendants, leaves, internal vertices and subtrees,
  and the fact that choosing a different root gives a different rooted tree;
- the level of a vertex and the height of a rooted tree;
- ordered rooted trees, and binary trees, with their left and right subtrees;
- the theorem that a tree with $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges;
- preorder, inorder and postorder traversal;
- expression trees, and the infix, prefix (Polish) and postfix (reverse Polish) forms of an expression,
  with parentheses needed only in the infix form;
- spanning trees, the theorem that a graph is connected if and only if it has a spanning tree,
  and the spanning trees that depth-first and breadth-first search build.

The notes define the traversals for ordered rooted trees, by pseudocode;
here they are defined recursively for binary trees, as lists,
and a remark extends preorder and postorder to ordered rooted trees.
In the notes a forest is not connected;
here a forest is any graph with no cycles, so a tree is a forest too.
The notes' $m$-ary trees, full $m$-ary trees, balanced trees, and the counting theorems for them,
siblings, back edges, and spanning forests of directed graphs are left out.
A bound on the number of vertices of a binary tree of a given height is in their place.
The definition of a parse tree is included from the
[mathematics prerequisites](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/) notes,
so it reads the same in both places.
Level order, as breadth-first search from the root, follows the course calendar's "tree traversal".
The proof that a tree with $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges, the other proofs,
the examples, the exercises and the Racket functions are new.
:::
